stimulus.text: Paraphrase of Michael Harrington, The Other America: Poverty in the United States (1962). Harrington wrote that forty to fifty million Americans lived in poverty, many in decaying urban slums and many in isolated rural towns. He noted that machines had taken work from people: the mechanization of agriculture and the automation of factory work displaced workers and left them in bitter poverty. His book helped shape the domestic agendas of President John F. Kennedy and his successor, President Lyndon Johnson.

rationales.A: Harrington counts forty to fifty million Americans in poverty even as the economy grew.
rationales.B: The passage counts millions still in poverty, so the growing economy had not ended it.
rationales.C: Harrington places the poor in decaying urban slums as well as in isolated rural towns.
rationales.D: Harrington blames the mechanization of farming and the automation of factory work, not the poor themselves.
rationales.general:
1. Harrington counts the poor: forty to fifty million Americans.
2. He places them in two settings: decaying urban slums and isolated rural towns.
3. That count comes from a time of general prosperity, which is the contrast he is making.
4. Poverty therefore persisted for millions even as the nation grew richer.
Remember: A big number beside a rich economy shows a gap, not a success.
